title: Probability in Medieval and Renaissance Philosophy

summaries.example: Imagine that two trusted coaches disagree about which team will win. You might think one answer is more believable, but you may still admit that the other answer is possible. Medieval thinkers often used “probable” for an idea that had good support but was not certain.
summaries.summary: Today, probability often means numbers between zero and one. Medieval and Renaissance thinkers used probability differently. They called an opinion probable when reasons, expert views, testimony, signs, or usual patterns gave it support. This did not mean the opinion was certainly true. People often had to decide what to do even when they could not know everything. Probable reasoning helped with debates, law, moral guidance, and practical choices. Medieval writers used words related to “probable,” “truth-like,” “believable,” and “frequent.” They also compared opinions: one could be more probable than another. Sometimes two opposing opinions were both called probable because different qualified people supported them. The entry follows these ideas from ancient sources through medieval scholastic thought and Renaissance humanism, while explaining that numerical probability came much later.
key_ideas: Medieval probability was usually about how believable or well-supported an idea was, not about numbers.
A probable idea was below complete knowledge or certainty, but it could still guide action.
People looked to experts, trusted reports, signs, and what usually happened when judging an idea.
These ideas were used in arguments, courts, moral decisions, medicine, and everyday life.
Renaissance humanists and medieval scholastics used many of the same words, although they sometimes emphasized different kinds of reasoning.
summaries.why_it_matters: This history shows that people have long needed to make responsible choices without perfect knowledge. It also reminds us that “probable” has not always meant a number. Understanding older meanings helps us see how ideas about certainty, disagreement, evidence, and risk changed over time.

important_terms.definition: An idea that has good reasons supporting it, even though it could still be wrong.
A belief or answer that someone accepts while knowing the opposite might be true.
A person’s report used as support for believing something happened.
A way of making a careful choice when complete certainty is not available.

questions_to_think_about: Can an idea be useful even when it is not certain?
Whom would you trust as an expert, and why?
Can two people reasonably support different answers?
Why might a court need rules for using clues and witnesses?

summaries.example: Suppose a court must decide whether a contract was broken. A witness may support one account, while other clues support another. Medieval legal thought could treat testimony or truth-like circumstantial evidence as giving a claim probability, but a single probable indication did not automatically settle the verdict. Several weaker indications might be combined, and stronger standards could be required for judgment.
summaries.summary: The entry reconstructs medieval and Renaissance probability as a family of qualitative practices rather than an early version of modern probability mathematics. Modern probability is quantitative and can be represented by numbers from zero to one, whereas medieval usage usually treated “probable” as a predicate of propositions, opinions, signs, or sometimes events. A probable proposition had enough support to justify assent or action but lacked the certainty associated with knowledge or full conviction. Between about 1200 and 1500, scholastic discussions developed several overlapping concepts. Endoxic probability derived from Aristotle’s account of reputable opinions: claims supported by everyone, most people, or suitably qualified experts. Proto-frequentist probability concerned what occurs usually or for the most part, although medieval examples may involve natural regularity, authority, or evidence rather than a modern frequency interpretation. Testimonial and juridical probability arose from witnesses, presumptions, and circumstantial signs. Semantic probability described a contingent relation in which a predicate belongs to a subject under most conditions without doing so necessarily. These notions supported dialectical syllogisms and practical deliberation. Medieval authors also used ordinal comparisons such as “more probable.” In debates, a proposition and its contrary could both be probable when different competent authorities supported them, a pattern that anticipates questions about reasonable disagreement. Renaissance humanists shared much vocabulary with scholastics but sometimes shifted attention from authority-based premises toward rhetoric, credibility, or the quality of an argumentative process. Numerical probability emerged only later, after further six
key_ideas: Pre-modern probability was primarily qualitative and often applied to propositions; it was not represented by numbers or governed by a probability calculus.
From roughly 1200 to 1500, the entry distinguishes endoxic, proto-frequentist, testimonial or juridical, and semantic conceptions of probability.
Endoxic probability connected acceptability with the opinions of many or of qualified experts, but authority could reflect both intellectual competence and social hierarchy.
Frequency expressions sometimes indicated what usually occurs, yet their precise relation to probability remains interpretively unsettled; they need not express modern frequentism.
Probable reasoning mattered because law, moral guidance, medicine, theology, rhetoric, and dialectic often dealt with uncertain premises.
Medieval thinkers could compare probabilities and acknowledge reasonable disagreement, even though they did not develop a full theory of this disagreement.
summaries.why_it_matters: The history clarifies that probability is not a single timeless concept. It can concern evidence, expert judgment, usual occurrence, confidence, or relations in the world. Studying medieval distinctions helps explain how philosophical communities handled uncertainty before calculation, and why modern debates about evidence, disagreement, risk, and objectivity have older roots.

important_terms.definition: A qualitative status assigned mainly to a proposition or opinion when evidence or recognized authority supports accepting it, without making it certain.
A proposition accepted as true while accompanied by awareness that the contrary may be true; it ranks below faith or knowledge in confidence.
A medieval conception in which a claim is probable because it is endorsed by everyone, most people, or qualified and reputable experts.
A debated interpretation of medieval claims that what happens usually or for the most part is probable; it is not yet modern numerical frequentism.
Probability arising from witnesses, presumptions, or circumstantial indicators in legal reasoning.
A conception of probability tied to contingent relations in things: a predicate belongs to a subject under most conditions but not by necessity.
A logical argument pattern whose premises are probable rather than certain, yielding a probable conclusion or opinion.
The medieval possibility that a proposition and its incompatible alternative could both be probable, often because different competent authorities supported them.

questions_to_think_about: Does widespread agreement make a claim probable, or does it merely make the claim persuasive?
How should expert authority be distinguished from institutional or social power?
Why might frequency be evidence for probability without being identical to probability?
Can two incompatible claims both be rationally acceptable from different perspectives?
What is gained, and what is lost, when qualitative judgments become numerical probabilities?

summaries.example: A doctor in a medieval town might have to choose a treatment without knowing exactly what would happen. A report from a trained doctor, a familiar sign, and what usually happened in similar cases could all support one choice. The choice would be reasonable if it was well supported, even though it was not guaranteed to work.
summaries.summary: Medieval and Renaissance philosophers had important ideas about probability, but they did not use probability as modern mathematics does. Today, probability is commonly represented with numbers and rules for calculating them. In the period studied here, a claim was more often called probable when it was believable, supported, or reasonable to accept, even though it was not certain. Medieval writers used several related words. Something could be “truth-like,” credible, or probable. A probable opinion was held with some caution because the thinker knew it might be mistaken. Scholars connected probability with respected authorities, skilled experts, witness reports, legal clues, and what usually happened. The entry groups major medieval ideas into four types. Endoxic probability came from opinions accepted by many people or by qualified experts. Proto-frequentist probability involved statements about what happened most of the time, although scholars debate whether these were really early versions of modern frequency theories. Testimonial and juridical probability concerned witnesses, presumptions, and evidence in legal settings. Semantic probability described things that were normally connected without being necessary. These forms of reasoning shaped university debates, legal decisions, moral advice, and practical life. Medieval thinkers could say that one opinion was more probable than another, and sometimes they allowed two opposing opinions to be probable when different competent people supported them. Renaissance humanists inherited much of this language but sometimes emphasized the strength and usefulness of an argument itself. The mathematical idea of probability appeared later.
key_ideas: Modern probability uses numbers, but medieval probability usually described degrees of believability or support in words.
A claim could be probable because respected experts accepted it, because evidence supported it, or because something usually happened that way.
Probability helped people act in uncertain situations, especially in law, moral guidance, medicine, and debate.
Medieval thinkers sometimes ranked one opinion as more probable than another.
Different people could support opposite opinions, and both opinions could still count as probable in a debate.
Renaissance humanists used many older terms but sometimes focused more on persuasive reasoning and credibility than scholastic writers did.
summaries.why_it_matters: People often must choose before they have complete proof. Medieval discussions show how thinkers tried to make those choices responsibly by weighing expertise, testimony, patterns, and arguments. They also help us understand why modern ideas such as evidence, uncertainty, risk, and reasonable disagreement are connected to much older questions.

important_terms.definition: Supported enough to be accepted or used, but not certain.
A belief held as true while recognizing that the other answer might be right.
A view supported by many people or by qualified experts.
Support based on what usually happens, though medieval writers did not mean the same thing as modern statistics.
Support supplied by witnesses, legal presumptions, or clues.
A relation in which something is usually connected with a feature, but not necessarily in every case.
A structured argument that begins with probable statements instead of certain ones.

questions_to_think_about: Is an expert’s opinion always stronger than your own observation?
Why might a clue count as support without proving something?
How is “usually happens” different from a percentage?
When two qualified people disagree, can both sides deserve serious attention?
Why would people need probability in everyday decisions?
